transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... it's about Garrett. I keep hearing his voice. It's just so clear, exactly like he’s standing right behind me when I'm out on the trail. The trails get incredibly muddy this time of year, actually. I had to buy these new hiking boots just last week—great arch support. Since I sit in a chair all day for my practice, you know, being a psychologist, I really need that physical support when I finally get outside to clear my head. 

But... where was I? Right, his voice. I hear him on the trail, or when I'm in my painting room. I’ve been doing a lot of watercolors lately, mostly landscapes, because the way the water bleeds the pigments together on the cold press paper is just... it's really fascinating how it takes on a life of its own. But anyway, he's just right there in the room with me. And even though the rational, educated part of me knows he’s dead... in the moment, it feels completely real.
Does hearing Garrett's voice cause you any distress?

Distress? Yeah, I mean... it's more than distress. It completely derailed everything. I actually had to stop seeing my own patients because I just couldn't practice safely anymore. I was cancelling sessions left and right, and the documentation... God, the documentation just piled up. You know how the new electronic health record systems are, they send you those automated alerts when a note is past due, and the interface is just so poorly designed. It takes five clicks just to enter a basic diagnostic code, which is ridiculous when you think about the volume of patients we're expected to see now. I was reading this article in a journal recently about physician burnout tied to EHRs, and it's staggering, really. 

But, right, the distress. It got so bad that my wife actually had to call crisis services. I just... I couldn't trust myself to be alone anymore. The voices, the whole thing... it was like everything just stopped. My practice, my home life, my own safety. Being admitted to the hospital, that was really the point where I realized everything had just stopped functioning.
Do you see things that other people do not see?

See things? No, no, I don't see anything that isn't there. It's just... it's just the hearing. Like I was saying, it's Garrett's voice. I hear him so clearly, like he's literally right over my shoulder when I'm out walking the trail or in my painting room. Speaking of the painting room, the lighting in there is just terrible. I bought these daylight-simulating LED bulbs online, the ones that are supposed to be 5000 Kelvin, because true color representation is so crucial when you're working with watercolors. If the light is too warm, your blues look muddy, and if it's too cool, the reds get completely washed out. I spent hours reading reviews on lighting setups for artists... 

Wait, what was I... right, Garrett. Yeah, I don't see him. I just hear his voice. And like I said, even though my clinical brain, the educated part of me, knows that he passed away... when I hear him in that room, or on the trail, it just feels so completely real in that exact moment. But no, I don't see him or anything else. Just the voice.
Do you find it difficult to stay on topic when talking about something?

Yeah, staying on topic... it's honestly exhausting. Because my thoughts just race so fast right now. I'll start with just one simple idea about a patient note, and then... well, speaking of notes, I actually use these specific fountain pens for my physical files. Japanese nibs, extra fine, because my handwriting tends to loop and get messy if the ink flow is too heavy. I order the ink directly from this little shop in Kyoto, they make this deep blue-black shade that is incredibly professional but still has a bit of character, you know? It takes weeks to ship, which is a nightmare with global supply chains lately, I was reading about the shipping container shortages... 

But sorry, what were we... right, the racing thoughts. So that one idea about a patient note instantly turns into five completely new projects I need to start, and then suddenly it morphs into a memory from a hike, and then before I can even catch any of it, I'm just drowning in guilt about the funeral. It all just flashes by in a matter of seconds, and I can't hold onto whatever it was I was originally trying to say.
How long have you been hearing Garrett's voice?

Well, this whole crisis... everything just started falling apart about a month ago, right after Garrett died. It's been about a month. Garrett and I actually used to track time by the hiking seasons, you know? Like, we'd know it was late October because the trail up to the ridge would get that specific kind of frost that crunches under your boots. I actually bought these new boots right before he passed, German-made, full-grain leather. You have to treat them with beeswax every season or the leather cracks where your toe bends. I spent a whole weekend just rubbing the wax in, using a hair dryer to melt it into the seams because if water gets in there, your socks are soaked for the rest of the hike. Merino wool socks help, of course, they wick the moisture away, but still... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, how long. Yeah, about a month. Ever since the funeral, really. That's when I started hearing him.
Do you often find that your thoughts don't make sense to you or others when you're speaking?

Make sense? No, no, I don't have that problem. I mean, my thoughts are moving incredibly fast, obviously, but they're completely logical. People understand me just fine. As a psychologist, communication is literally my profession, so I have to be articulate. I actually presented at a seminar just last spring on therapeutic communication barriers. We held it at this hotel downtown, and the acoustics in the conference room were just abysmal. They had these cheap lavalier microphones that kept picking up static from the Wi-Fi routers. 

I actually have a bit of a hobby with audio equipment, and I tried to tell the AV guy he needed to switch the frequency channel to avoid the interference. I use a high-fidelity condenser mic at home for dictating my patient session notes, and it connects via an XLR cable rather than USB. The analog-to-digital conversion is just so much cleaner that way, and you don't get that weird digital compression artifacting that makes your voice sound all tinny. You really need a dedicated audio interface to power it, though, because it requires 48 volts of phantom power... 

Sorry, I lost the thread there. What were you asking? Oh, if my thoughts don't make sense to people. No, I don't think so. I know I'm talking a lot, and maybe bouncing around, but I'm definitely not speaking gibberish. Everything I'm saying makes perfect sense.
Is Garrett's voice something you hear all the time, or does it come and go?

It's not all the time, no. It really only started happening during that... that intensely wired stretch, you know? When I was barely sleeping at all but felt completely driven to just keep going, taking on all those impossible projects. I had never heard him like that before my mood took this massive shift. It definitely wasn't just a normal part of grieving for me. 

But speaking of projects, I actually decided during that time to completely redesign my home office. I ripped up all the carpet myself because I wanted to lay down this reclaimed oak hardwood. I found a supplier who salvages wood from old barns in Pennsylvania, and the grain pattern is just incredible. It has all these natural imperfections and nail holes that give it so much character. I bought a specialized pneumatic flooring nailer just for the job, one that uses L-cleats instead of staples because they hold the wood tighter as it expands and contracts with the humidity. You really have to leave a quarter-inch expansion gap around the perimeter, though, or the whole floor will buckle in the summer when it gets humid. I actually installed a dedicated hygrometer in the room just to monitor the moisture levels... 

Sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, Garrett's voice. Yeah, it only happens when I'm in that really elevated, non-stop state. Not before that.
Does Garrett's voice ever tell you to do things or give you commands?

Commands? No, no, he doesn't tell me to do things. It's more just... I came in because I keep hearing his voice as clearly as if he's standing right behind me on the trail, or in my painting room. And even though part of me knows he's dead, in the moment, it feels completely real. 

Speaking of the painting room, I actually just bought this incredible set of Kolinsky sable brushes. The hair comes from a specific type of weasel in Siberia, and the snap on the bristles is just unmatched. You can hold a massive amount of water in the belly of the brush, but it still comes to a perfect, razor-sharp point. I've been using them for watercolors, mostly landscapes, trying to capture the way the light hits the ridge at dawn. You have to use 100% cotton rag paper, though, preferably 300-pound cold press, or the water just warps the paper and ruins the wash. I stretch my own paper using gummed paper tape on a wooden board, which is a whole process. You have to soak the paper in a tub for exactly ten minutes, then lay it flat and tape the edges down while it's still soaking wet. As it dries, it pulls drum-tight, so when you finally apply the paint... 

Wait, sorry. Did I answer your question? You were asking if Garrett tells me to do things. No, it's not commands. It's just his voice, clear as day, like he's right there with me.
Do you feel like you're able to express your thoughts in a straightforward and organized way when you're talking to someone?

Organized? I mean, I try to be. But lately, it's just... my thoughts race so incredibly fast. It's like, I'll have one idea about writing up a patient note, and before I even finish the sentence in my head, it turns into five different projects I need to start, and then a memory of a hike I took last year, and then this crushing guilt about the funeral, all before I can even catch a single thread of it. 

I actually used to go hiking up at Mount Rainier every summer. We'd take the Wonderland Trail, which is just this brutal 93-mile loop around the volcano. You have to get a backcountry permit months in advance because they limit the number of hikers to protect the alpine meadows. The elevation gain is insane—you're constantly climbing up these ridges and dropping back down into river valleys. I bought this ultra-lightweight titanium camping stove for the trip because every ounce matters when you're carrying your life on your back for ten days. It runs on isobutane canisters, and it boils a liter of water in under three minutes, which is crucial when you're freezing at 6,000 feet and just want to rehydrate your freeze-dried chili. You have to be careful with the wind, though, so I fashioned a windscreen out of heavy-duty aluminum foil... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, being organized when I talk. Yeah, it's hard when my brain is just firing off a million things at once.
Do you think your racing thoughts and jumping between topics are related to your mood or emotional state?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, they definitely started around the same time. At first, I felt almost lit up, like I had this urgent purpose that no one else could see or understand. But then if anyone questioned me or tried to slow me down, I would just snap into this absolute rage. 

It’s kind of like when you’re driving a manual transmission and you try to downshift too fast. I used to have this vintage 1974 BMW 2002, the one with the round taillights, not the square ones they introduced later. I spent an entire summer rebuilding the dual Weber carburetors on that thing. You have to tune them perfectly, balancing the airflow between the two barrels using this special snail-type synchronizer meter. If the mixture is even slightly too lean, the engine will run hot and you risk burning an exhaust valve, but if it’s too rich, it just bogs down and fouls the spark plugs. I ended up upgrading the ignition system to an electronic distributor because the old mechanical points would constantly wear down and throw the timing off. I’d spend hours on Sunday mornings just adjusting the valve clearances with a feeler gauge, making sure they were exactly eight thousandths of an inch... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Mood? Right, yeah. The racing thoughts definitely tie into that feeling of being completely lit up and then suddenly furious. It all kind of hit at once.
Have you ever had a period of time where you didn't hear Garrett's voice at all since it started?

A period where I didn't hear it? Well, I mean, I didn't hear him at all before this whole thing started. I only started hearing Garrett’s voice during that really wired stretch when I barely slept and felt completely driven to keep going. I had never heard him like that before the mood shift—it definitely wasn’t something that happened during just ordinary grief. It was only when my brain sped up and I started taking on all those impossible projects. 

Like, I decided out of nowhere to completely rebuild a commercial espresso machine in my kitchen. I found this beat-up La Marzocco Linea on Craigslist, and I was up for days tearing it down. It has this massive dual boiler system, and you have to pull out the copper heating elements and soak them in a citric acid bath to descale them. But you have to monitor it constantly, because if you leave it in the solution too long, the acid will actually pit the copper and ruin the boiler's integrity. I was rewiring the entire machine to install a custom PID temperature controller so I could keep the brew water at exactly 201.5 degrees. If you're pulling a shot of a really dense, light-roast single-origin bean, even a half-degree drop in temperature will completely under-extract the coffee and leave it tasting sour and thin. I even bought a specialized bottomless portafilter and a distribution tool with these 0.3-millimeter acupuncture needles to break up the clumps in the grounds before tamping, just to make sure the extraction was perfectly even across the puck... 

Wait, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Oh, if there was a time I didn't hear him. Yeah, I didn't hear him before that sleepless, wired phase. That's when it all actually started.
Have you ever lost touch with reality for a period of time since you started hearing Garrett's voice?

Lost touch with reality? I don't... I mean, I don't think so? It feels real to me. The voice, the drive, all of it. I don't feel like I'm floating away or anything. But I guess reality is sort of subjective, right? 

Like, take photography. I got really obsessed with large-format film photography a while back. I bought this massive 8x10 wooden field camera, the kind where you have to put a dark cloth over your head just to see the ground glass to focus. You don't just snap a picture; you have to calculate the exposure using the Zone System, figuring out exactly how you want the shadows and highlights to fall on the negative. And then you have to develop the sheet film in total darkness. I was using this developer called Pyrocat-HD, which actually stains the film emulsion and gives you these incredibly sharp, contrasty negatives that are perfect for platinum/palladium printing. The printing process is insane—you have to hand-coat heavy watercolor paper with a mixture of ferric oxalate and actual precious metal salts, then expose it under a UV light source. I built a custom UV exposure unit out of an old tanning bed I found at a thrift store. I had to strip out all the wiring and replace the ballasts to run these specific BLB fluorescent tubes, because if the wavelength isn't exactly right, the image just washes off when you put it in the clearing bath...

Wait, sorry. Reality. Yeah, no, I don't think I've lost touch with reality. I just... things have been really intense.
Have you ever felt like Garrett's voice is a part of your own thoughts, rather than someone else's voice?

No, it doesn't feel like my own thoughts at all. It's not like an internal monologue or me just remembering him. I hear him as clearly as if he’s standing right behind me, like when I'm out on the trail or in my painting room. Even though part of me logically knows he's dead, in that exact moment, it feels completely real. 

Speaking of painting, I actually completely reorganized my studio last week because I decided I needed to grind my own oil paints from raw pigments. You can't just mix the powder with linseed oil; you have to use a glass muller on a frosted glass slab and work it in a figure-eight motion for, like, an hour just to get one color right. The particle size of the pigment dictates how much oil it needs to bind properly. Like, ultramarine blue is incredibly thirsty, but if you're making lead white—which you have to be so careful with because of the toxicity, I had to buy a specialized respirator just to handle the dry powder—it takes barely any oil at all. I was trying to recreate this specific medium that the old Dutch masters used, which involves boiling the linseed oil with litharge, which is a lead monoxide, and then adding a tiny bit of Venice turpentine to give it this enamel-like quality. You have to cook it outside on a hot plate because if it catches fire, it's basically napalm. I spent three days straight just adjusting the proportions and testing the drying times on these little canvas swatches, making sure it didn't wrinkle the paint film...

Wait, sorry. I'm drifting again. But yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely not my own thoughts. It's his voice, clear as day, like he's right there in the room with me.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely high or euphoric, even if things were not going well in your life?

High? I mean, at first I felt almost lit up, like I had this incredible, urgent purpose that no one else could see. It was amazing. But the flip side was that I would just snap into absolute rage if anyone questioned me or tried to slow me down. I had zero patience for anyone operating at a normal speed. 

Like when I decided I needed to completely rebuild a vintage Roland Juno-106 synthesizer. The guy I bought it from said it was beyond repair, but he just didn't understand the circuitry. The main issue with those old boards is the 80017A voice chips—they coated them in this factory resin back in the eighties that degrades over the decades and shorts out the internal components. You can't just buy original replacements, so I spent days carefully desoldering all six chips from the printed circuit board. You have to be incredibly precise, using a specialized vacuum desoldering pump, because if you apply too much heat with the iron, you'll lift the copper traces right off the board and permanently ruin the whole voice architecture. Then I had to soak the chips in a pure acetone bath in a glass jar for exactly 48 hours to dissolve that resin without eating into the silicon. I actually built a makeshift ventilation hood in my dining room just to deal with the fumes. And calibrating it afterward is a nightmare—you have to hook it up to a digital oscilloscope and adjust these tiny trimpots on the motherboard to make sure the pulse width modulation and the filter resonance are perfectly in phase across all six voices. If even one is off by a fraction of a volt, the chords sound completely muddy and out of tune...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing the thing again. What were we talking about? Euphoric, right. Yeah. I felt incredibly lit up and driven, but just... pure rage if anyone interrupted my focus or told me to stop.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely energetic and didn't need much sleep, but still felt rested and able to function?

Yeah, the sleep thing... for weeks, I was sleeping maybe two or three hours a night, tops. And I wasn't tired at all. I felt completely wired, like my brain was running on high-voltage electricity. 

That's actually when I got really into cultivating rare orchids in my basement. I realized the humidity in the house was completely wrong for epiphytic orchids, specifically the *Bulbophyllum* species, which need like 80% humidity and constant air movement to prevent fungal rot. So I stayed up for three days straight building this automated Wardian case out of extruded aluminum and tempered glass. I had to wire up an Arduino microcontroller to run a series of ultrasonic foggers and micro-fans. You can't just use regular tap water for the foggers, either, because the mineral buildup will clog the ceramic discs and burn out the ultrasonic transducers, plus the dissolved solids are toxic to the orchid roots. So I had to install a reverse osmosis filtration system under the utility sink, tapping directly into the copper pipes, which meant I had to learn how to sweat copper joints with a propane torch and lead-free solder. I spent hours researching the exact vapor pressure deficit needed for optimal stomatal opening in the leaves. And then I had to mount the orchids onto these slabs of natural cork bark, tying them down with barely visible fishing line and packing the roots with live sphagnum moss that I had to source from this specific bog in New Zealand, because the domestic stuff breaks down too quickly and turns acidic...

Sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? The sleep. Right. So I was sleeping two or three hours and feeling totally wired. But lately, it's changed. Now I'm crashing into this really broken, heavy sleep, but it doesn't help. I still wake up exhausted and just... panicky, usually way before dawn, and I can't get back to sleep.
Have you felt overwhelmingly sad or hopeless for an extended period since Garrett's death?

Sad? Hopeless? Um... I don't know if I'd use those exact words. It's more like this crushing weight, this absolute void where everything used to be. It's not just a feeling, it's like a physical pressure in the room.

Speaking of pressure, I started roasting my own coffee beans because I realized the atmospheric pressure in the house was affecting the extraction yield of my espresso. You can't just buy pre-roasted beans; they start off-gassing carbon dioxide the second they leave the roaster, and within two weeks, all the volatile aromatic compounds are basically gone. So I bought this commercial-grade fluid bed roaster, but the heating element wasn't precise enough, so I had to bypass the factory thermostat and wire in a PID controller with a K-type thermocouple probe that sits directly inside the bean mass. You have to monitor the rate of rise—the RoR—constantly, because if the temperature increases too fast before the first crack, you'll scorch the outside of the bean while the inside stays underdeveloped and tastes like wet grass. But if you stall the roast, you bake the beans and they taste like cardboard. I spent an entire weekend charting these roast curves on my laptop, adjusting the fan speed and heat input second by second to hit exactly 405 degrees Fahrenheit at exactly nine minutes and thirty seconds. And then you have to cool them instantly—I built a custom cooling tray with a high-velocity centrifugal fan to pull ambient air through the beans so they don't keep roasting from their own internal heat...

Wait, sorry. I'm sorry. I lost the thread again. What was it you asked? Sadness? Hopelessness? Yeah, I don't know. I just... I don't know if I'd call it that. It's just a heavy, heavy void.
Have you ever felt like you were unstoppable or invincible during one of these periods of high energy and decreased need for sleep?

Unstoppable? Invincible? No, I wouldn't say that. I didn't feel like a superhero or anything, just... really, really capable. Like my brain was finally firing on all cylinders and I could just see how everything connected. 

That's when I realized how flawed modern mechanical watch movements actually are. Most people think a Swiss escapement is the pinnacle of engineering, but they don't realize how much energy is lost to friction in the pallet fork. So I bought a bunch of vintage pocket watch movements off eBay—mostly old Elgins and Walthams from the 1920s—and decided to machine my own co-axial escapement. You can't just use standard tools for that. I had to buy a jeweler's lathe and retrofit it with a digital readout system. The tolerances are absurd—we're talking microns. I spent, I don't know, maybe four days straight just trying to turn a balance staff out of high-carbon steel. You have to temper it perfectly, heating it until it turns this exact shade of straw-yellow, and then quench it in oil, otherwise the pivots will just snap under the tension of the mainspring. And don't even get me started on poising the balance wheel. You have to use these tiny timing screws, filing off microscopic amounts of weight from the underside of the screw heads until the wheel rests perfectly still in any position on the poising tool. If it's heavy on one side, the watch will run fast when it's dial-up and slow when it's crown-down...

Sorry, I'm rambling again, aren't I? I just... I get so caught up in the details. What were we talking about? Oh, feeling invincible. No, I didn't feel invincible. Just... capable. Really capable.
Have you ever had a period where your thoughts and feelings seemed completely disconnected from reality, lasting for more than a day?

Disconnected from reality? Um... I guess that depends on what you mean by reality. I mean, I know what reality is supposed to be, but... actually, that's why I came in. I keep hearing Garrett's voice. Like, as clearly as if he's standing right behind me. It happens when I'm out on the trail, or when I'm in my painting room. 

Speaking of the painting room, I had to completely overhaul the lighting in there recently. You see, standard LED bulbs have a terrible Color Rendering Index—the CRI. Most of them peak way too high in the blue spectrum and have this massive dip in the cyan and red frequencies, which completely washes out the subtle undertones of cadmium red and ultramarine blue. If you're trying to mix a true neutral gray using complementary colors, a low CRI light will make it look muddy and green. So I had to track down these specialized full-spectrum Solux halogen bulbs, which mimic natural daylight at exactly 4700 Kelvin. But they run incredibly hot, so I couldn't just put them in regular fixtures. I had to build these custom aluminum heat sinks and wire in active cooling fans, which meant calculating the thermal resistance of the thermal paste and making sure the airflow CFM was high enough to dissipate the wattage without creating a wind tunnel effect in the room that would dry out my acrylics too fast on the palette. I even built a wet palette using a specific semi-permeable membrane—I had to order this industrial baking parchment from France because the domestic stuff is coated in silicone, which repels the water instead of letting it wick through the sponge...

I'm sorry. I'm doing it again. The voice. Right. Garrett's voice. Even though part of me knows he's dead... in the moment, when I hear him, it feels completely real. Like he's just... right there.
Have you ever had a period where you heard Garrett's voice and also saw things that weren't there at the same time?

Like I was just saying, the voice is really the whole reason I came in. I keep hearing Garrett’s voice as clearly as if he’s standing right behind me on the trail or in my painting room. And even though part of me knows he’s dead, in the moment it feels completely real. But seeing things? Um... I don't think I've ever actually seen him, or anything else that wasn't there. It's just the voice. 

Speaking of the trail, though, I actually had to completely redesign my hiking boots for that specific ridge where I keep hearing him. The soil composition up there is mostly decomposed granite, which acts like microscopic ball bearings underfoot. Standard EVA foam midsoles don't have the torsional rigidity for that kind of scree, and the factory lugs on most boots are angled for mud, not rock. So I bought a cobbler's anvil and started resoling my own boots. You can't just glue new rubber on; you have to strip the old sole, rough up the leather with a wire wheel on an angle grinder, and then apply a specialized toluene-based contact cement. But the cement needs to cure at exactly 70 degrees with low humidity, otherwise the solvent gets trapped and the bond fails under shear stress. I ended up building a miniature climate-controlled curing chamber out of an old mini-fridge, wiring in a ceramic heating emitter and a dehumidifier hooked up to a smart relay system so I could monitor the vapor pressure deficit from my phone. I spent about a week mapping out the optimal lug geometry on CAD software before I even ordered the Vibram sheets, because if the spacing is off by even a millimeter, the self-cleaning property of the tread is completely compromised and you just end up carrying three pounds of dirt on your feet...

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You asked if I saw things. No, I haven't seen anything. It's just... I just hear him. Like he's right there.
Have you ever had a period where your thoughts and feelings seemed completely disconnected from reality for more than a day, but then returned to normal?

Returned to normal? Well, I guess... yeah, I mean, the voice stopped when that whole wired phase ended. I only started hearing Garrett's voice during that stretch when I was barely sleeping and taking on all those impossible projects, just feeling totally driven to keep going. I had never heard him like that before my mood shifted like that, and it wasn't just... it wasn't like ordinary grief. It was only during that high-energy time. 

Which, actually, was when I decided I needed to completely digitize and cross-reference my entire library of psychological journals. Because the standard indexing systems like PsycINFO are so incredibly inefficient if you're looking for longitudinal correlations across disparate methodologies. So I bought a high-speed planetary book scanner—the kind they use in archival libraries—but the stock image processing software was garbage. It kept skewing the text recognition if the pages had even a slight curvature near the binding. So I had to teach myself Python and write a custom optical character recognition script using a neural network library. I spent, God, maybe five days awake just feeding it training data, manually correcting the bounding boxes on thousands of pages so the algorithm could learn to compensate for the page warp. I even had to build a custom cradle out of extruded aluminum and 3D-printed brackets to hold the books at exactly a 110-degree angle, because if you open an old hardcover to 180 degrees, you'll crack the spine and ruin the binding glue. And speaking of binding glue, modern perfect binding is just a tragedy compared to Smyth sewing...

Wait. Sorry. I'm doing it again. The voice. Right. Yeah, it stopped when that whole intense period stopped. It was just during that time when I couldn't sleep and couldn't stop working.

I even built a wet palette using a specific semi-permeable membrane—I had to order this industrial baking parchment from France because the domestic stuff is coated in silicone, which repels the water instead of letting it wick through the sponge...

I'm sorry. I'm doing it again. The voice. Right. Garrett's voice. Even though part of me knows he's dead... in the moment, when I hear him, it feels completely real. Like he's just... right there.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where you heard Garrett's voice and also saw things that weren't there at the same time?

patient.answer:
Like I was just saying, the voice is really the whole reason I came in. I keep hearing Garrett’s voice as clearly as if he’s standing right behind me on the trail or in my painting room. And even though part of me knows he’s dead, in the moment it feels completely real. But seeing things? Um... I don't think I've ever actually seen him, or anything else that wasn't there. It's just the voice. 

Speaking of the trail, though, I actually had to completely redesign my hiking boots for that specific ridge where I keep hearing him. The soil composition up there is mostly decomposed granite, which acts like microscopic ball bearings underfoot. Standard EVA foam midsoles don't have the torsional rigidity for that kind of scree, and the factory lugs on most boots are angled for mud, not rock. So I bought a cobbler's anvil and started resoling my own boots. You can't just glue new rubber on; you have to strip the old sole, rough up the leather with a wire wheel on an angle grinder, and then apply a specialized toluene-based contact cement. But the cement needs to cure at exactly 70 degrees with low humidity, otherwise the solvent gets trapped and the bond fails under shear stress. I ended up building a miniature climate-controlled curing chamber out of an old mini-fridge, wiring in a ceramic heating emitter and a dehumidifier hooked up to a smart relay system so I could monitor the vapor pressure deficit from my phone. I spent about a week mapping out the optimal lug geometry on CAD software before I even ordered the Vibram sheets, because if the spacing is off by even a millimeter, the self-cleaning property of the tread is completely compromised and you just end up carrying three pounds of dirt on your feet...

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You asked if I saw things. No, I haven't seen anything. It's just... I just hear him. Like he's right there.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where your thoughts and feelings seemed completely disconnected from reality for more than a day, but then returned to normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I only started hearing Garrett’s voice during that wired stretch when I barely slept, took on impossible projects, and felt driven to keep going. I had never heard him like that before the mood shift, and it wasn’t something that happened during ordinary grief.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timing of psychotic symptoms (being disconnected from reality) to determine if they occur independently of mood episodes, which corresponds to the requirement that hallucinations occur exclusively during the manic episode.

patient.answer:
Returned to normal? Well, I guess... yeah, I mean, the voice stopped when that whole wired phase ended. I only started hearing Garrett's voice during that stretch when I was barely sleeping and taking on all those impossible projects, just feeling totally driven to keep going. I had never heard him like that before my mood shifted like that, and it wasn't just... it wasn't like ordinary grief. It was only during that high-energy time. 

Which, actually, was when I decided I needed to completely digitize and cross-reference my entire library of psychological journals. Because the standard indexing systems like PsycINFO are so incredibly inefficient if you're looking for longitudinal correlations across disparate methodologies. So I bought a high-speed planetary book scanner—the kind they use in archival libraries—but the stock image processing software was garbage. It kept skewing the text recognition if the pages had even a slight curvature near the binding. So I had to teach myself Python and write a custom optical character recognition script using a neural network library. I spent, God, maybe five days awake just feeding it training data, manually correcting the bounding boxes on thousands of pages so the algorithm could learn to compensate for the page warp. I even had to build a custom cradle out of extruded aluminum and 3D-printed brackets to hold the books at exactly a 110-degree angle, because if you open an old hardcover to 180 degrees, you'll crack the spine and ruin the binding glue. And speaking of binding glue, modern perfect binding is just a tragedy compared to Smyth sewing...

Wait. Sorry. I'm doing it again. The voice. Right. Yeah, it stopped when that whole intense period stopped. It was just during that time when I couldn't sleep and couldn't stop working.
